title: Monotonic deque
sub: The maximum of every window in O(n): who can be forgotten for good, and what to use instead of the Deque<T> .NET lacks
cards/0/title: The problem: the maximum of every window
cards/0/body:
Sliding Window Maximum (LeetCode #239, hard). Given an array nums and a number k, a window of length k slides from left to right one element at a time; return the maximum at every window position — n − k + 1 numbers in total. Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, −10⁴ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴, 1 ≤ k ≤ n.

Example: [1, 3, −1, −3, 5, 3, 6, 7], k = 3 → [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7].

It is a fixed-size window, but the “add the incoming, subtract the leaving” trick fails: you cannot “subtract” a maximum. Window [3, −1, −3], the 3 leaves — who is the maximum now? You need to remember the next candidates, and not all of them, only those that still stand a chance.

Signals: the maximum or minimum at every window position — fixed or variable (for example, “the longest subarray where max − min ≤ limit”). In a game: the worst frame over the last N frames, the highest terrain cell within a radius, the peak threat over the last k AI ticks.
cards/1/q: Where do you need the maximum or minimum over a sliding window? Select all.
cards/1/options/0: The worst frame time over the last 120 frames, updated every frame
cards/1/options/1: The longest subarray where max − min ≤ limit
cards/1/options/2: The average frame time over the last 120 frames
cards/1/options/3: The largest number in the whole array
cards/1/options/4: The lowest price over every k consecutive days
cards/1/explain: The worst frame is a maximum over a fixed-size window, the lowest price over k days is a minimum over a window. max − min ≤ limit is a variable-size window that needs both the maximum and the minimum. The average is a sum with subtraction, no deque needed. The maximum of the whole array is a single pass with no window at all.
cards/2/title: Brute force and O(n log k) solutions
cards/2/body:
Brute force: scan k elements for every window — O(n·k). With k ≈ n/2 and n = 10⁵ that is ≈ 2.5·10⁹ comparisons — too slow.

An ordered set. Keep the window’s elements in a SortedSet — a red-black tree: insertion and removal are O(log k), the maximum is the rightmost node. The trap: SortedSet is a set, so equal values collapse into one. Window [3, 1, 3]: the first 3 leaves, you remove 3 — and the second 3, still in the window, is gone too. So store the pair (value, index): the pairs are distinct, and tuples compare by the first field, then the second. The result is O(n log k), memory O(k).

A heap. A max-heap with lazy deletion: push (index, value), and before answering discard everything at the top that has left the window. No removal from the middle of the heap is needed, but stale elements can pile up — O(n log n) and O(n) memory. PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority> exists since .NET 6; Unity does not have it, but it does have SortedSet.

Either is a fine first answer in an interview. But the interviewer will ask: can you do it in O(n)?
cards/3/q: Why put the pair (value, index) into the SortedSet rather than just the value?
cards/3/options/0: A set collapses equal values: removing the 3 that left would also lose the other 3 still in the window
cards/3/options/1: Without the index, SortedSet cannot compare the elements
cards/3/options/2: The index is needed for Max to run in O(1)
cards/3/explain: SortedSet stores each value once: Add of the second 3 returns false and adds nothing. When the first 3 leaves, Remove(3) deletes the only entry, and the window [1, 3] is left without its 3. A pair with the index makes every window element unique.
cards/3/wrong/1: ints are comparable as they are. The problem is not comparison but that equal values are one entry of the set.
cards/3/wrong/2: SortedSet.Max walks to the rightmost node of the tree, O(log k) with or without the pair.
cards/4/title: The key idea: who can be forgotten for good
cards/4/body:
Let j < i and nums[j] ≤ nums[i]. Then j will never be the maximum again: every future window that contains j also contains i — it is further right and leaves later — and its value is no smaller. Such a j can be thrown away immediately.

Who remains? Candidates with nobody greater or equal to their right. Keep their indices in a deque — a queue you can push to and pop from at both ends:

— the indices in the deque increase, and the values strictly decrease;
— nums[i] arrives — pop from the back everyone ≤ it, then push i to the back;
— the index at the front has left the window (≤ i − k) — pop it;
— the window maximum is at the front.

Why O(n): every index enters the deque once and leaves at most once — at most 2n operations in total, just like the left edge of the window in the previous lessons. The deque holds at most k indices — memory O(k).

At most one index leaves from the front per step: only i − k drops out of the window. That is why it is an if there, not a while.
cards/5/q: Assemble the deque solution. The deque is an array plus two indices: the live part is dq[head..tail−1].
cards/5/explain: The window is [i − k + 1..i], so index i − k is already outside it: the condition is <=. Pop from the back everyone not greater than the new value: that keeps the deque values strictly decreasing. The maximum is at the front, nums[dq[head]]. At most one index leaves from the front per step, so an if is enough; a while would also be correct. No ring is needed: every index is pushed once, an array of length n suffices, and head only grows.
cards/6/task: Step through the trace on [2, 7, 4, 1, 3, 6, 5, 8], k = 3. The rig stops twice before a new number arrives and asks what the deque does first.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: The deque is [1, 2, 3] — values 7, 4, 1. i = 4, x = 3 arrives. What does the code do first?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: The front comes first: index 1 ≤ i − k = 1, the 7 has dropped out of the window [2..4] and leaves. Only then the back: the 1 ≤ 3 is popped, the 4 is greater than 3 and stays. The deque becomes [2, 4], and the window maximum is 4.
cards/6/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: Pushes index 6 (value 5) to the back: deque [5, 6]
cards/6/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: Pops index 5 from the front and pushes 6
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: The deque is [5] — value 6. i = 6, x = 5 arrives. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: Only those ≤ the new value are popped from the back: 6 > 5, so the 6 stays. Index 5 has not dropped out of the window [4..6]. The 5 goes to the back: it is smaller than the 6 for now, but the 6 leaves earlier — at i = 8 — and then the 5 may become the maximum. The deque values still decrease: 6, 5.
cards/7/q: On nums = [5, 1, 1, 1], k = 2 this code returns [5, 5, 1] instead of [5, 1, 1]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/7/explain: At i = 2 the window is [1..2], and index 0 with the 5 must leave: 0 ≤ 2 − 2. The < condition does not pop it, so the 5 stays the maximum of a window of length k + 1. Index i − k is the first one already outside the window, hence <=.
cards/8/title: .NET has no deque: what to use instead
cards/8/body:
The .NET standard library has no Deque<T>. What it has, and why it does not fit:

— Queue<T> is a circular array, but you can only remove from the front: popping the back is impossible;
— Stack<T> — only the top;
— List<T>.RemoveAt(0) shifts the whole array — O(n) per operation;
— LinkedList<T> does everything in O(1): AddLast, RemoveLast, RemoveFirst, First, Last. But every AddLast is a new node object on the heap (about 48 bytes for an int on 64-bit), the nodes are scattered in memory, and they are garbage for the collector. In Unity with the Boehm GC, such code running every frame shows up.

Your own deque on a circular array: an array, a head index and a count. With a power-of-two capacity, “wrapping around” is & (Length − 1) instead of %. Every operation is O(1), growth by doubling is amortised O(1), as with List<T>. After warm-up there are no allocations.

#239 itself does not even need that: every index is pushed once, so an array of length n and two indices are enough — head only grows, no ring required. Your own deque is needed when the number of elements in the stream is not bounded in advance — say, in a game that runs for hours.
cards/9/q: Deques in .NET and Unity. Which statements are true? Select all.
cards/9/options/0: LinkedList<T> gives O(1) at both ends but allocates a node object on every add
cards/9/options/1: Queue<T> works as a deque: it can remove from the back
cards/9/options/2: In a deque on a circular array with capacity 2ᵏ the wrapped index is computed with & (Length − 1)
cards/9/options/3: List<T>.RemoveAt(0) is O(1) because there is an array inside
cards/9/options/4: For #239 an array of length n with two indices is enough, no ring needed
cards/9/explain: LinkedList is a doubly linked list: operations at the ends are O(1), but every node is a heap object. Queue<T> can only remove from the front. The mask only works for a power-of-two capacity: x & (2ᵏ − 1) is x mod 2ᵏ, and for −1 it also gives the last index. RemoveAt(0) shifts every element — O(n). In #239 every index is pushed once, so an array of length n suffices, and head only grows.
cards/10/title: Where else a deque works, and when it is not needed
cards/10/body:
A variable-size window + two deques (LeetCode #1438): the longest subarray where max − min ≤ limit. One deque keeps the maximum candidates (values decrease), the other the minimum candidates (values increase). When the window is bad, move l and pop from the fronts any indices that fell below l.

Negative numbers (LeetCode #862): the shortest subarray with sum ≥ k. The window from lesson 2 breaks here; what works is prefix sums plus a deque of indices with increasing prefixes — the same principle of “throw away whoever will never be useful again”.

Unity: inflating obstacles on a grid by the agent radius with a square kernel. A cell becomes blocked if the (2r + 1)×(2r + 1) square around it contains an obstacle — that is a maximum over a window: first along rows, then along columns. The deque gives O(W·H) for any radius instead of O(W·H·r²).

When a deque is overkill. The worst frame over the last 120 frames is 120 comparisons per frame — microseconds. A plain scan of the ring buffer is simpler and harder to get wrong. A deque pays off when the window is large and there are many steps: n and k around 10⁵, large grids, server metrics.
cards/10/deep:
The exact count. In #239 every index is pushed to the back once and popped at most once — from the back or the front. So there are at most 2n deque operations in total, even though a single step may pop k − 1 elements. It is the same amortised argument as for the left edge of the window and for the monotonic stack (the stacks unit): a deque is a monotonic stack whose “bottom” also leaves the window.

Heap versus deque in memory. With lazy deletion the heap keeps elements that have left the window until they surface at the top. On a decreasing array the top is always the oldest element, and it leaves on time. On an increasing array the new element is always on top while the old ones pile up below — up to n elements, though the window holds k. The deque holds at most k.

Cache and Burst. A deque on an array is sequential memory, with no pointers and no GC. In a Burst job the same solution is written on a NativeArray<int> with two indices — managed collections are not available there. Inflating obstacles row by row parallelises naturally: every row is an independent task (IJobParallelFor over rows, then over columns).

Why a tuple works in SortedSet. ValueTuple<int, int> implements IComparable: compare by the first field, then by the second on a tie. The default comparer uses it, with no boxing.
cards/11/q: Match each approach to the window maximum with its cost.
cards/11/pairs/2/1: O(n log n) and up to O(n) memory
cards/11/pairs/4/1: O(n), but a node object per element
cards/12/q: You are solving Sliding Window Maximum out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: k ≤ n, how many numbers to return, whether there are repeats
cards/12/items/1: Name the O(n·k) brute force and why a sum with subtraction does not work here
cards/12/items/2: Offer O(n log k): a SortedSet of (value, index) pairs — and the trap with repeats
cards/12/items/3: The O(n) idea: a left element no greater than a right one is never the maximum again — a deque of decreasing values
cards/12/items/4: Write the code: front left the window — pop; back ≤ x — keep popping; push i; answer from the front
cards/12/items/5: Run [1, 3, −1, −3, 5, 3, 6, 7], k = 3, showing the deque at every step
cards/12/items/6: Complexity O(n): every index enters and leaves once; .NET has no Deque<T> — an array with two indices
cards/12/explain: The O(n log k) solution is an honest stepping stone: the interviewer sees you know the cost of collections and will ask for better. Then the domination idea, the code, a run and the complexity with the “enters and leaves once” argument. Mention the missing Deque<T> in .NET yourself — it is a platform-knowledge question.
